units: the writer answers a complaint from the reader about poor sleep
the writer has spoken to a nurse at a care centre
the advice falls into three separate groups
the first group concerns what is eaten in the evening
a shortage of iron is presented as a source of lasting tiredness
the second group covers physical activity and stretching
the third group describes the conditions of the bedroom
the nurse advises seeking help if the spells come back
the writer asks for news of whatever has been tried
text: You say your evenings are restless and that sleep keeps slipping away from you. I put the question to a nurse at the centre I go to, and she sorts her advice into three groups. The first is about what goes on the plate at night: no heavy meal close to bedtime, and she reminded me that a shortage of iron keeps a stubborn tiredness going. The second is about moving: a walk each afternoon, a slow stretch of the shoulders once the light goes, nothing strenuous as night draws near. The third is the bedroom itself, which she wants cool, dark and quiet, with no screen left glowing. One remark stayed with me: if the dizziness or the shivering comes back, do not sit it out, go and be seen. Write and tell me what you have tried, and I will say whether it matches what she described.

units: a patient being interviewed describes the stages of her recovery
the first sensation mentioned is a heaviness in the limbs
a state of queasiness then arrives in waves
the first week seemed to her to have no end
the second week went by almost unnoticed
quiet and half-light helped her to improve
a nurse kneaded the back of her neck at the close of the day
a wound on her arm that was slow to heal worried her more than her diagnosis
she advises asking nothing of oneself
text: What comes first? The patient being interviewed describes a dull heaviness, as though her limbs had doubled in weight. And after that? The queasiness arrives, she says, a wave that rises and pulls back without warning. Does that stage last? She hesitates, then answers that the first week seemed to have no end, while the second slipped past almost without trace. What eased it? Quiet, half-light, and the hand of a nurse who came to knead the back of her neck as the day closed. And the nights? Sleep came back in pieces, never whole. Did she fear she would not mend? She admits that a wound on her arm was slow to close, and that this one detail troubled her more than the whole diagnosis. And her advice at the end? Ask nothing of yourself, and take slowness as an ally rather than an enemy.

units: a sports doctor explains a chain of causes to his patient
a muscle that has not been prepared stays cold and short of give
a cold fibre tears more readily under a sudden stretch
the tear brings on inflammation in that spot
the inflammation draws blood in and sets off the pain
the patient wonders about the swelling of his knee
the swelling comes from the same chain of events
cold laid on the area eases the process
using the joint too soon holds up the healing
text: The sports doctor sets out for his patient how one thing leads to the next. Skipping the warm-up, he explains, leaves the muscle fibres cold and short of give. The patient asks what difference that makes in practice. A cold fibre takes a sudden stretch badly, the doctor answers, and tears without much resistance. The tear then brings on inflammation in that spot, he adds, which draws blood towards it and sets off the pain. The patient wonders aloud about the swelling that has come up around his knee. That swelling belongs to the same chain, the doctor tells him, and a cold pack laid on the area will settle it. A muscle properly prepared, he reminds him, takes the jolts without giving way. He ends by warning that healing will drag on if the joint is used too soon, and he advises building the training back up by degrees.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in former times slight wounds killed patients with no other illness
those who treated them saw fever and discharge without grasping where it began
infection was held at the time to be unavoidable
observers noticed a difference between the wards
the wards where hands went unwashed lost more patients
the measure adopted was the cleaning of hands and instruments
the measure was poorly received at first by those who did the caring
the mortality records ended up convincing them
the rule remains a foundation of care
text: There was a time when slight wounds carried off patients whom nothing else threatened. Those who treated them saw the fever, the shivering, the discharge, without ever tracing where the grim sequence began. The obstacle lay in a belief: infection was held to be unavoidable, almost part of the natural order. Patient observers came at last upon an unsettling regularity, for the wards where hands went unwashed lost more of their patients than the others. The remedy, austere in its plainness, was to clean the hands and the instruments before every procedure. It met sharp resistance, since the demand quietly laid blame on those who did the caring. The mortality records won the argument in the end, and the deaths fell away. That modest rule still stands as one of the pillars of care.

units: two closely related sensations are often mixed up
one gives the illusion that the room is turning
the other feels like an inward giving way with no turning
the first has its origin in the inner ear
the inner ear tells the brain how the head is tilted
the second comes from a brief drop in the blood supply to the brain
with the first it is best to sit down and fix the eyes on something still
with the second one should lie flat and raise the legs
a repeat of these episodes warrants a medical examination
text: Two sensations that lie very close together are constantly mixed up. In the first of them, the room seems to turn around you; in the second, something gives way inside, with no turning at all. The turning kind starts in the inner ear, which tells the brain how the head is tilted. The other comes from a brief drop in the blood supply reaching the brain. What helps is therefore not the same, and anyone who confuses them delays the response that would actually help. When the room turns, sit down, fix your eyes on something still and keep the neck from moving. When everything seems to drain away, lie flat and raise the legs, so that blood is brought back towards the head. A single episode of either sort means little on its own, but one that keeps returning deserves a medical examination.

units: the narrator recounts a stay at a spa centre
the treatments included bubbling baths and clay wraps
a therapist kneaded his back with some force
he describes the other guests he met there
a teenager had been sent there by his lung specialist
the food lacked flavour but was served with solemnity
he slept better than he had done in a very long while
he left lighter and convinced that rest is something you learn
text: Right, let me tell you about my week at the spa centre, because the whole thing was well worth the trip. The treatments first: bubbling baths, clay wraps, and a therapist who kneaded my back until I laughed out of sheer pain. Then the other guests: a former swimmer who talked without drawing breath, a retired woman who knew every corridor, a teenager sent along by his lung specialist and sulking about it. Then the meals: bland, honestly, but served with a gravity that made the blandness feel almost ceremonial. And the nights: I slept as I had not slept in ages, no jolting awake, no knot in the throat. The heavy hush of the corridors must have had a hand in that. I came home lighter, faintly ridiculous in a dressing gown too short for me, and sure that rest is something you learn.

units: the first check concerns the state of the shoes
a worn sole throws the stride off and wears at the knees
a warm-up of wide movements comes before the run
the calves and the thighs are loosened without forcing
the start is made at a pace that still allows talking
the speed goes up only after the first third of the route
the stop must be gradual and followed by walking
a lukewarm shower settles the muscles on returning
a sharp pain in a knee calls for skipping the next session
text: Begin by looking over your shoes: a worn sole throws the stride off balance and wears at the knees. Then give the warm-up a dozen wide movements, enough to lift the heart rate without any jolt. Loosen the calves and the thighs, never forcing a stiff joint. Set off at a steady pace, one you could hold while talking out loud. Pick the speed up only once the first third of the route is behind you. At the end, do not stop dead: keep walking, let the breath come down, drink in small spaced mouthfuls. Tell someone your route if you are heading out alone as the light fades. Once you are home again, a lukewarm shower is enough to settle the muscles. Drink again half an hour after stopping. If a sharp pain shows up in a knee, give the next session a miss and have somebody look at it.

units: there are not enough seats in the waiting room of a clinic
the closure of a nearby surgery has shifted its patients to this place
the wait before an appointment has grown longer
consultations have become shorter
questions left unanswered bring patients back once more
a care assistant says she recognises the same faces far too often
minor troubles worsen for want of steady follow-up
the management announces two more practitioners for the warm season
text: Since the autumn there have not been enough seats in the waiting room of the clinic. The surgery down the road closed, its whole list washed up here, and the effect has spread outwards ever since. Appointments drift further off, so consultations grow shorter; shorter consultations leave questions hanging, so patients come back. A mother who brought her son leaves with one question in three answered. A care assistant speaks of faces she recognises far too often. Without steady follow-up, small troubles worsen in silence: a deficiency left untreated, a wound that will not close, a blood pressure climbing with no warning. The management says two more practitioners will arrive when the warm season comes. Until then the most pressing cases are dealt with first, and everyone senses that the backlog will fall due later.

units: a first aid kit fits into a rigid case held shut by a strap
the main difficulty comes from the muddle and not from the contents
one searches through it at a moment when the hands are shaking
the answer is to split the equipment between labelled compartments
the first compartment holds what is needed to clean a wound
the second gathers dressings bandages and round-tipped scissors
the third houses gloves a survival blanket and a medical notebook
the notebook sets out current treatments and allergies
the case is kept near the front door so that a visitor can find it
text: A well-judged first aid kit fits into a rigid case that is held shut by a strap. The usual trouble is not what goes into it but the muddle inside: you rummage through it just when your hands are shaking. The answer to that is to split the contents up between clearly labelled compartments. The first takes the sterile dressings and the solution for cleaning a wound. The second holds plasters in several sizes, elastic bandages and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The third keeps disposable gloves, a folded survival blanket and a notebook setting out current treatments along with any known allergies. A recent prescription can be slipped in beside it. Kept near the front door of the home, the case stays within easy reach even for a visitor who does not know the place at all.

units: two directions of care are set against one another
the first acts once the illness has declared itself
its effect can be seen without difficulty
the second steps in before the disorder appears
its results stay out of sight since they consist of illnesses avoided
this difference in visibility explains the gap in funding
the writer holds that preventing costs less and spares suffering
the writer asks that both directions be funded equally
text: We are too quick to set the medicine that repairs against the medicine that prevents, as though one had to hand over its resources to the other. The first steps in once the illness has declared itself: it operates, prescribes, relieves, and its effect can be measured without difficulty. The second acts before any disorder appears, and its results stay out of sight, since they consist of illnesses that never happened. That imbalance of visibility explains the imbalance of the budgets. Repair can be seen; prevention cannot. Yet it ought to be granted that prevention costs less and spares whole tracts of suffering, while repair tends to arrive late. Our health institutions should fund both paths with the same steadiness, instead of treating the second as an optional extra.
